edges.description: Tick inoculation can expose early macrophage and monocyte targets to viable rickettsiae.
Bite-site infection can produce a necrotic eschar.
Monocyte/macrophage survival precedes dissemination to the intracytosolic niches that sustain endothelial infection.
Systemic rickettsial spread can extend infection to microvascular endothelium.
Cytosolic R. helvetica remains dependent on bacterial ribosomal protein synthesis.
Endotheliotropic infection and inflammatory signaling drive systemic fever.
Systemic inflammation can present as headache.
Systemic inflammation can present as myalgia.
Systemic inflammation can present as arthralgia.
Systemic rickettsial endothelial infection can produce a rash.
Endotheliotropic infection can involve cardiac tissue.
R. helvetica has been implicated in lymphocytic meningitis.
Cardiac rickettsial infection can present as myocarditis or perimyocarditis.
Meningeal inflammation manifests clinically as meningitis.

nodes.description: Arthralgia can accompany the acute R. helvetica febrile illness.

evidence.reference_title: Aneruptive fever associated with antibodies to Rickettsia helvetica in Europe and Thailand.
evidence.snippet: Clinical symptoms included fever, headache, and arthralgia in all patients, myalgia in four, and an inoculation eschar in one but no cutaneous rash.

nodes.description: Rare disseminated R. helvetica infection can involve pericardial, coronary, and myocardial tissue, with chronic interstitial inflammation and endothelium-localized rickettsia-like organisms in reported sudden-cardiac death cases.

evidence.reference_title: Association of Rickettsia helvetica with chronic perimyocarditis in sudden cardiac death.
evidence.snippet: Examination of PCR-positive tissue showed chronic interstitial inflammation and the presence of rickettsia-like organisms predominantly located in the endothelium.

nodes.description: In the early post-inoculation phase, monocytes/macrophages can be exposed before vascular endothelial infection is established. In a THP-1 human monocytic model, R. helvetica survived, propagated, and induced TNF-alpha, supporting monocytes as an early host-cell compartment in the pathograph.

nodes.description: Suspected R. helvetica disease is treated with doxycycline, a cell-penetrant tetracycline that reaches the rickettsial cytosolic niche and inhibits bacterial 30S ribosomal translation; post-bite prophylactic doxycycline is not recommended for asymptomatic tick exposure.

nodes.description: Spotted-fever-group rickettsiae disseminate from the bite site and target microvascular endothelium, producing focal small-vessel vasculitis; in R. helvetica infection this conserved mechanism is kept narrow because most reported human disease is mild and aneruptive.
